title: Death stopped for me
hookLine: because I could not stop for Death, he kindly stopped for me
tomorrow: why would a poet tell you to tell the truth crooked?

cards: A packed calendar says no to almost everything: no time, maybe next month. Dickinson's carriage poem begins with exactly that excuse, and someone comes anyway.
"Because I could not stop for Death, He kindly stopped for me; The carriage held but just ourselves And Immortality." Death, as a gentleman caller. He brings a carriage.
He's polite. And she gets in.

teach.h: WE SLOWLY DROVE, HE KNEW NO HASTE.
teach.b: The ride is slow. "We slowly drove, he knew no haste," and she puts away her work, and her leisure too, for his civility.
They pass a school where children play at recess. They pass fields of grain, gazing back at them. They pass the setting sun.

teach.h: A HOUSE LIKE A SWELLING OF GROUND.
teach.b: Then they pause at a house that seems a swelling of the ground, its roof barely showing: a grave. And the last stanza jumps.

It has been centuries since then, she says, and yet they feel shorter than that one day, when she first guessed the horses' heads were turned toward eternity. So the speaker is telling all this from the far side.
That's the teaching of the poem. Death isn't a thief who grabs.
He's a courteous escort who stops for the person too busy to stop for him, and the road runs past all of life, childhood, harvest, sunset, on its way to eternity.
Readers argue over whether the ride is a comfort or a chill, and the poem leaves room for both. But it does one clear thing: it makes death civil, unhurried and kind, a caller rather than a raid.

how: Some readers of Dickinson read this poem at memorials and in classrooms, slowly, stanza by stanza, the way the carriage moves.

games.q: what does “death stopped for me” mean?
o: a play Dickinson staged at home with her family
Dickinson's poem of Death as a kind escort in a carriage
a coach driver who took Dickinson to church on Sundays

games.q: a slow ride with a polite driver: tap the pairs.

s: in the poem, Death snatches the speaker away
he kindly stops, and drives slow, with civility.
the ride passes children at recess, fields of grain and the setting sun
all of life, on the way.
the poem is told on the day of the ride
the last stanza says it has been centuries.

games.q: a classmate says her grandmother, who is dying, seems calm, and asks if that's denial. what fits Dickinson's poem?
o: some people meet death as a kind escort; her calm can be real, not denial.
calm always means a person doesn't understand what's happening.
the poem says death should be fought to the very end.
games.why: Dickinson's speaker rides beside Death with civility on both sides. a calm goodbye can be a true one.

practice: If you can, take a slow walk, even just across the room and back, at the carriage's pace: he knew no haste. Notice what you pass, a window, a plant, the light. Let the slowness be the whole point.

wordCard.voice: Death stopped for me: Dickinson's carriage ride, where Death is a kind, unhurried escort for someone too busy to stop, heading toward eternity.

carryVoice: Take this with you: he kindly stopped. In Dickinson's ride, death comes as a courteous caller, not a thief. See you tomorrow.
